about: How much greenhouse gas things emit, in CO₂-equivalent (CO₂e, 100-year GWP). Values are typical figures from life-cycle studies and official inventories; every card says what is included and links the original study. Where a source gives only energy, CO₂e is computed with the grid factor stated on the card.
gridNote: AI and data-centre energy is converted at 0.4 kg CO₂e per kWh, roughly the average grid where most data centres run (US/China mix), unless the source gives CO₂e itself.

totals.gtNote: Excluding land use and forestry (JRC/IEA). Including land use, UNEP puts 2025 at about 58.4 Gt CO₂e.

pies.label: By sector
pies.title: Global emissions by sector, 2025
pies.note: Direct emissions by where they happen (JRC/IEA, 54.1 Gt CO₂e excluding land use). Electricity counts under power, not under the buildings or factories that use it. Shares are rounded; power is given as “nearly 30%”.

pies.label: By country
pies.title: Global emissions by country, 2025
pies.note: Territorial emissions excluding land use (JRC/IEA). International shipping and aviation belong to no country. Rest of world is the remainder.

categories.label: Major offenders
categories.blurb: Whole sectors and industries, per year. These are the slices of the pie.

categories.label: AI
categories.blurb: Prompts, images, video, agents, training runs and the data centres behind them. Figures move fast: companies only began disclosing in 2025.

categories.label: Digital
categories.blurb: Devices, streaming, search, email and crypto.

categories.label: Transport
categories.blurb: Per kilometre, per trip and per vehicle.

categories.label: Food
categories.blurb: Per kilogram of product, farm to retail (Poore & Nemecek 2018, the largest meta-analysis: about 38,700 farms).

categories.label: Goods & materials
categories.blurb: Things you buy and the bulk materials they are made of.

categories.blurb: Average footprint of one person per year, and the 1.5 °C reference.

items.name: AI chatbot text prompt (typical)
items.water: 0.26–0.32 mL disclosed by Google and OpenAI; 45 mL in Mistral's full life cycle
items.scope: Data-centre side of one ordinary text answer: chips, servers, idle capacity, cooling. Not your phone or the network. The high end (Mistral, 1.1 g) also spreads training and hardware manufacturing over every answer.
items.summary: A few tenths of a watt-hour: about a microwave running for one second. Three independent numbers now agree (Google measured, OpenAI stated, Microsoft modelled).
items.context: Google's median Gemini prompt fell 33-fold in energy and 44-fold in CO₂e in one year, mostly through software efficiency and clean-power contracts. The 0.03 g Google figure is market-based (counts its clean-energy purchases); on an average grid the same 0.24 Wh is about 0.1 g.
tips: Use a small/fast model for simple questions; reasoning modes cost 10–100× more.
Ask once with full context rather than many short retries.
Per prompt it is tiny; what matters is billions of prompts and ever-larger models.

items.name: Gemini text prompt (Google, measured)
items.energy: 0.24 Wh (0.10 Wh for the AI chips alone)
items.scope: Measured in Google's production fleet: active TPUs, host CPU and memory, idle reserve machines and data-centre overhead. Excludes network, your device and training. Market-based emissions.
items.summary: The first detailed, measured per-prompt figure from a major provider (Aug 2025). Less energy than nine seconds of television.
items.context: Location-based (actual grid), the same energy is about 0.1 g CO₂e. The AI chips are only 58% of the energy; the rest is servers, idle capacity and cooling, which earlier chip-only estimates missed.
tips: Image and video prompts are not covered by this figure and cost far more.

items.name: ChatGPT query (OpenAI, stated)
items.scope: Figure stated by OpenAI's CEO in June 2025, without published method. CO₂e computed here at 0.4 kg/kWh.
items.summary: About what a high-efficiency light bulb uses in a couple of minutes. Earlier widely quoted '3 Wh per query' (2023) was about ten times too high for today's systems.
items.context: Independent bottom-up estimates (Epoch AI ≈0.3 Wh) agree for short answers. Long, reasoning-heavy GPT-5-class answers have been benchmarked at 18 Wh on average and up to about 40 Wh.
tips: Pick the non-reasoning mode for lookups and rewording.

items.name: Le Chat answer, full life cycle (Mistral)
items.scope: Peer-reviewed life-cycle analysis (with Carbone 4 and ADEME, AFNOR Frugal AI method): includes training, inference and manufacturing of servers and buildings, allocated per answer. Excludes your device.
items.summary: The most complete per-answer figure published (July 2025), and why it is about ten times Google's: it includes the model's training and the hardware's manufacturing.
items.context: Training plus 18 months of use of Mistral Large 2 totalled 20.4 kt CO₂e and 281,000 m³ of water. Mistral runs mostly in France, on a low-carbon grid.
tips: This boundary is the honest one to compare with other products' life cycles.

items.name: AI reasoning / long-answer prompt
items.energy: ≈3.9 Wh median (≈5,000 output tokens); 33 Wh or more for long prompts on the heaviest models
items.scope: Data-centre energy modelled from model size, hardware and measured API speed. CO₂e at 0.4 kg/kWh.
items.summary: Thinking models write thousands of hidden tokens before answering, so one prompt costs 10–100 ordinary ones.
items.context: In a 30-model benchmark, reasoning models used over 33 Wh on a long prompt, 70× the smallest model on the same task. Even so, a 10-minute hot shower takes about 2–3 kWh of heat, so a heavy reasoning prompt is roughly 1% of one shower.
tips: Turn reasoning on only when the task needs it.
Reasoning is where AI's energy growth per user comes from.

items.name: AI agent task (coding agent, deep research)
items.energy: ≈10–400 Wh: dozens to hundreds of model calls, each re-reading a long context
items.scope: Estimate built from per-token energy of long, high-reasoning prompts (≈34 Wh for 10,000 input + 1,500 output tokens) times typical agent step counts. No provider discloses agent energy yet.
items.summary: One multi-step agent job can equal hundreds of chat prompts, because every step re-reads the growing context.
items.context: Still small next to physical activities: a heavy agent task is around a kilometre in a petrol car. But agents run unattended and at scale, which is why research on carbon-aware agent scheduling started in 2026.
tips: Give agents tight scope and the files they need, so they loop less.
Prefer providers that publish energy and run on clean grids.

items.name: AI image generation
items.energy: ≈0.6–1.2 Wh (1024×1024, Stable Diffusion 3, incl. server overhead); 2.9 Wh average across older models
items.scope: Data-centre energy for one image on open models, measured. CO₂e at 0.4 kg/kWh.
items.summary: A few times a text prompt: about five seconds of a microwave.
items.context: Image models cost roughly the same regardless of prompt length; resolution and step count drive energy. Doubling quality roughly doubled energy in MIT Technology Review's tests.
tips: Generate at the size you need; upscale only the keeper.

items.name: AI video, 5 seconds
items.energy: ≈944 Wh (3.4 MJ) measured on an open model; 7–214 Wh reported for other open models
items.scope: Data-centre energy measured on open models; frontier closed models (Sora, Veo) do not disclose. CO₂e at 0.4 kg/kWh.
items.summary: The heavy end of consumer AI: one short clip can equal a thousand or more text prompts, roughly a microwave running for an hour.
items.context: Energy grows faster than clip length: a six-second clip used four times a three-second one in one study. Estimates span 100×, so treat the central value as an upper-range indication.
tips: Draft with images or storyboards, render video last.
Shorter clips at lower resolution cut energy more than proportionally.

items.name: A heavy AI user for a year
items.scope: Worked example: 30 text prompts and 5 reasoning prompts every day, plus a few images a week. CO₂e at 0.4 kg/kWh, data-centre side only.
items.summary: About 20 km in a petrol car, or 0.03% of a Swiss resident's yearly footprint. Individually small; collectively it is what drives data-centre growth.
items.context: Add agents and video and the figure can rise several-fold. The device you use (its manufacture especially) usually outweighs your prompts.
tips: Keeping your phone or laptop one extra year saves more than a year of prompts.

items.name: Training GPT-3 (2020)
items.scope: Electricity of the final training run only (Patterson et al. 2021, with Google). Excludes experiments, failed runs, hardware manufacturing.
items.summary: 552 t CO₂e: about 290 Zürich–New York return flights. Small by today's standards.
items.context: Training runs have grown roughly 4–5× in compute per year since; the largest 2025 run (Grok 4) is estimated at about 270× GPT-3's emissions.

items.name: Training GPT-4 (2023, estimated)
items.scope: Outside estimate from leaked/estimated GPU-hours; OpenAI has not disclosed. CO₂e at 0.4 kg/kWh.
items.summary: Around 10,000 t CO₂e, roughly 20 times GPT-3.
items.context: Treat as order of magnitude. Researchers stress that what labs disclose is shrinking even as the runs grow.

items.name: Training Llama 3.1 405B (Meta, 2024)
items.energy: ≈30 GWh (39.3 million H100-hours for the whole 3.1 family)
items.scope: Location-based, from Meta's model card (the 405B model alone). Meta reports zero market-based emissions because it matches its use with renewable purchases.
items.summary: 8,930 t CO₂e: about 690 Swiss residents' yearly footprint, for one model.
items.context: Open models get fine-tuned thousands of times by others; those derivative footprints are not counted anywhere yet.

items.name: Mistral Large 2: training + 18 months of use
items.scope: Full life-cycle analysis: training, inference, servers, buildings, end of life. Training and inference are reported together (85.5% of the total).
items.summary: 20.4 kt CO₂e for a 123-billion-parameter model, including all its use for a year and a half.

items.name: Training Grok 4 (xAI, 2025, estimated)
items.scope: Epoch AI estimate for the final run, assuming the on-site gas turbines that power the Colossus cluster in Memphis. Excludes experiments and serving.
items.summary: ≈150 kt CO₂e: the electricity of a town of 4,000 Americans for a year, or a large passenger jet flying for three years.
items.context: The largest disclosed-or-estimated training run to date, about 270× GPT-3. Gas-fired power makes it several times dirtier than the same run on a clean grid.
tips: Location matters: the same run on Swiss or French power would emit about a tenth.

items.name: AI GPU board, manufacture (NVIDIA HGX B200)
items.scope: Cradle-to-gate product carbon footprint (ISO 14067, by WSP): materials, assembly and transport of the baseboard with 8 GPUs. Excludes the rest of the server (CPUs, memory, power supplies), the data centre and use.
items.summary: 2.3 t CO₂e, about 285 kg per GPU before it ever runs. Memory and chips dominate.
items.context: Running it is far bigger: at about 8–10 kW for a few years, use-phase electricity is typically 50–150 t CO₂e on an average grid. NVIDIA reports 24% lower embodied carbon per unit of compute than the H100 generation.

items.name: All data centres in the world
items.energy: 415 TWh in 2024 (1.5% of world electricity); ≈945 TWh projected for 2030
items.scope: Indirect CO₂ from electricity, all workloads (AI is a fast-growing subset). Excludes backup generators and building/hardware manufacture.
items.summary: ≈180 Mt CO₂: about 0.5% of energy CO₂, a fifth of aviation. Growing about 15% a year, rising to roughly 300 Mt by 2035 in the IEA base case.
items.context: Small globally but concentrated: in the US data centres account for nearly half of electricity demand growth to 2030, and AI servers grow about 30% a year. Gas and renewables supply most new demand; several tech firms are contracting nuclear, including restarts and SMRs.
tips: The climate effect depends on the grid: siting and clean firm power matter more than per-prompt efficiency.

items.name: A 1 GW AI data-centre campus for a year
items.scope: Computed: 1 GW × 8,760 h × emission factor. Central at 0.4 kg/kWh; low end on nuclear/hydro (≈0.012 kg/kWh life cycle), high end on coal (≈0.95).
items.summary: ≈3.5 Mt CO₂e a year: the domestic emissions of about 900,000 Swiss residents. Several such campuses are being built.
items.context: The fuel choice changes the result 80-fold, which is why the power deals behind AI campuses matter more than chip efficiency claims.

items.name: Web search
items.scope: Data-centre side only. Google has not updated its 2009 disclosure; searches with AI overviews add an AI prompt.
items.summary: Similar to an AI text prompt, contrary to the early claim that chatbots cost ten times a search.

items.name: Email
items.scope: Typing, sending and storing, including a share of devices (Berners-Lee). Spam ≈0.03 g, a short email ≈0.3 g, one with a large attachment up to ≈26 g.
items.summary: Tiny per message; the device you write it on is most of it.
tips: Unsubscribing from newsletters is fine housekeeping, but not a climate lever.

items.name: Video streaming, one hour
items.scope: Data centre, networks and viewing device (European average, Carbon Trust). A large TV dominates; a phone is far lower.
items.summary: About 55 g per hour, mostly your screen. Early claims of several kg per hour were off by about 50×.
tips: Watch on the smallest screen that is comfortable; Wi-Fi over mobile data.

items.name: Smartphone, whole life
items.scope: Life cycle from manufacturer reports (e.g. Apple product environmental reports): production, transport, charging over 3–4 years, end of life.
items.summary: About 60 kg, and around 80% of it is spent before you switch it on.
items.context: Charging a phone every day for a year is about 4–5 kWh, a couple of kg CO₂ even on a dirty grid.
tips: Keep it longer: going from 3 to 5 years cuts its yearly footprint by about 40%.
Buy refurbished; repairable models (Fairphone) report ≈40 kg.

items.name: Laptop, whole life
items.scope: Manufacturer life-cycle reports (Apple, Dell, Lenovo): production, transport, 4 years of use, end of life.
items.summary: A few hundred kg, mostly from making the chips, screen and memory.
tips: Extend its life with a battery swap; buy refurbished.

items.name: Bitcoin network
items.scope: Electricity of mining, from the Cambridge industry survey (2025), which found about half the power from sustainable sources. Other trackers estimate up to about twice the emissions.
items.summary: ≈40 Mt CO₂e a year: about Switzerland's entire domestic emissions, for one payment network. Per data-centre energy, roughly a third of all data centres.
items.context: Ethereum cut its energy by over 99% in 2022 by switching to proof-of-stake; Bitcoin's design ties security to energy spent.

items.name: Petrol car, per km
items.scope: Fuel burned plus fuel production (UK government factors, average car). The high end adds the car's manufacture spread over its life (ICCT).
items.summary: About 200 g per km. Two people in the car halves it per person.
tips: Share rides; switch to train or e-bike for trips under 10 km.
An EV on the Swiss grid cuts this by about two-thirds.

items.name: Electric car, per km
items.scope: Life cycle incl. battery manufacture. Low end on a hydro/nuclear grid like Switzerland's, high end on a coal-heavy grid (ICCT global comparison).
items.summary: Lower than a petrol car on every major grid; on Swiss power about a third.
items.context: The battery adds 3–5 t at the factory, paid back after roughly 15,000–25,000 km in Europe.

items.name: Making a petrol car
items.scope: Cradle-to-gate: steel, aluminium, plastics, assembly (ICCT and manufacturer LCAs).
items.summary: About 7 t before the first kilometre, roughly half a Swiss resident's yearly footprint.

items.name: Making an electric car
items.scope: Cradle-to-gate incl. battery; battery cells made with coal power sit at the high end.
items.summary: About 4 t more than a petrol car at the factory, recovered within two to three years of normal driving in Europe.

items.name: Short-haul flight, per km
items.scope: Economy, incl. the extra warming of contrails and NOx at altitude (UK government factors with radiative forcing). Without it, about half.
items.summary: Per km a bit below driving alone, but flights cover distances you would never drive.
tips: Zürich–Paris, Milan or Munich by train cuts emissions by over 90%.

items.name: Flight Zürich–London return
items.scope: ≈1,580 km × short-haul factor incl. non-CO₂ effects.
items.summary: About a quarter of a tonne: what a year of driving 1,200 km produces.

items.name: Flight Zürich–New York return
items.scope: ≈12,600 km × long-haul economy factor incl. non-CO₂ effects. Low end: CO₂ only. High end: business class (≈3× the floor space).
items.summary: About 1.9 t: one flight is roughly 15% of a Swiss resident's whole year, and close to the 2.5 t per-person 1.5 °C budget for 2030.
tips: Fewer, longer trips; economy; direct routes (take-off is fuel-heavy).

items.name: Flight Zürich–Tokyo return
items.scope: ≈19,200 km × long-haul economy factor incl. non-CO₂ effects. Low end CO₂ only; high end business class.
items.summary: About 2.8 t, more than an Indian resident's whole year.

items.name: Train, per km
items.scope: Operation plus a share of infrastructure. Swiss and French electric rail sit at the low end; diesel-heavy networks at the high end (UK government factors: national rail ≈35 g).
items.summary: About 20 times lower than driving alone in Switzerland.

items.name: Bus or coach, per km
items.scope: Diesel coach ≈27 g, average city bus ≈100 g (UK government factors). Electric buses far lower.
items.summary: A long-distance coach is one of the lowest-carbon ways to travel after the train.

items.name: E-bike, per km
items.scope: Manufacture of bike and battery spread over its life, plus charging (European Cyclists' Federation method). A normal bike is similar once the rider's extra food is counted.
items.summary: Around 15 g per km, a tenth of a petrol car.

items.name: One-week cruise
items.scope: Ship fuel per passenger (heavy fuel oil or LNG incl. methane slip), excluding flights to the port.
items.summary: Roughly a transatlantic return flight, per person.

items.name: Beef (beef herd)
items.scope: Farm to retail: land-use change, methane from digestion, manure, feed, processing, transport, packaging. Global mean of the meta-analysis; the range is between producers.
items.summary: The single most carbon-intensive common food: about 100 kg per kg, 30× tofu.
items.context: Beef from dairy herds averages 33 kg per kg, because the cow also produces milk. Transport is under 1% of beef's footprint: what you eat matters far more than local.
tips: Swap half your beef for chicken, pork or legumes.
If you buy beef, dairy-herd beef has about a third of the footprint.

items.name: Beef (dairy herd)
items.scope: Farm to retail; emissions shared with milk.
items.summary: A third of beef-herd beef.

items.name: Lamb and mutton
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: Second only to beef among meats: sheep are ruminants too.

items.name: Cheese
items.scope: Farm to retail. About 10 litres of milk go into 1 kg of hard cheese.
items.summary: More than pork or chicken per kg, though eaten in smaller amounts.
tips: Fresh cheeses (mozzarella, ricotta) use less milk per kg than hard cheeses.

items.name: Dark chocolate
items.scope: Farm to retail. Driven by forest clearing for cocoa in West Africa and Latin America; the spread is huge.
items.summary: Surprisingly high on average, entirely because of deforestation. Deforestation-free cocoa is a fraction.

items.name: Coffee beans
items.scope: Farm to retail, as for chocolate driven by land-use change.
items.summary: High per kg, but a cup uses only about 7–10 g of beans.

items.name: Cup of coffee
items.scope: Computed: about 8 g beans at the mean bean footprint, plus brewing. Milk drinks add ≈0.2–0.3 kg for a 200 mL latte.
items.summary: A black coffee is roughly a kilometre in a car; a latte roughly two.
tips: The milk in a latte is often more than the coffee; oat milk cuts it by about two-thirds.

items.name: Prawns (farmed)
items.scope: Farm to retail; mangrove clearing for ponds drives the high end.
items.summary: Close to cheese, and well above chicken or farmed fish.

items.name: Pork
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: An eighth of beef.

items.name: Chicken
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: A tenth of beef; most of it is feed.

items.name: Farmed fish
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: Similar to pork.

items.name: Eggs
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: About 0.3 kg per egg.

items.name: Cow's milk
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: About three times plant milks (oat ≈0.9, soy ≈1.0).

items.name: Rice
items.scope: Farm to retail. Flooded paddies release methane.
items.summary: The highest-carbon staple grain, about three times wheat, because of paddy methane.

items.name: Tofu
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: About a thirtieth of beef for similar protein.

items.name: Wheat and bread
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: Low.

items.name: Peas and beans
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: Among the lowest-carbon proteins: they fix their own nitrogen.

items.name: Bananas
items.scope: Farm to retail, incl. shipping from the tropics.
items.summary: Low even after crossing an ocean: shipping by sea is efficient.

items.name: Potatoes
items.scope: Farm to retail.
items.summary: One of the lowest-carbon foods.

items.name: Wine
items.scope: Farm to retail; glass bottles are a large share.
items.summary: About 0.27 kg per 150 mL glass.

items.name: 1 kWh of electricity
items.scope: World average generation (≈470 g). Swiss production ≈30 g; Swiss consumption mix incl. imports ≈100–130 g; EU ≈240 g; coal ≈950–1,000 g; nuclear and wind ≈5–13 g life cycle.
items.summary: The grid you plug into changes the answer 80-fold. This one number drives every electricity-based figure here.
items.context: Life-cycle (UNECE) per kWh: coal ≈1,000 g, gas ≈430–490 g, solar ≈8–83 g, hydro ≈6–147 g, wind ≈8–16 g, nuclear ≈5–6 g.

items.name: Boiling 1 litre of water
items.scope: Computed from the energy to heat 1 L from 15 °C plus losses, on the world-average grid; Swiss mix ≈0.01 kg.
items.summary: One kettle is roughly 300 ordinary AI prompts.

items.name: Hot shower, 10 minutes
items.energy: ≈2–3 kWh of heat (≈80 L warmed by 25 °C)
items.scope: Computed: gas boiler ≈0.5 kg; oil ≈0.7; heat pump on Swiss power ≈0.05.
items.summary: One hot shower ≈ thousands of AI prompts. Hot water is one of the bigger household items.
tips: A low-flow head (6 L/min) and one minute less saves about a third.

items.name: Washing machine load (40 °C)
items.scope: Electricity only, computed; Swiss mix at the low end. Detergent and machine manufacture add a little.
items.summary: Small: heating the water is most of it.
tips: Wash at 30 °C and line-dry: a tumble dryer load is several times a wash.

items.name: Tumble dryer load
items.scope: Electricity only, computed.
items.summary: One of the hungriest appliances per use.

items.name: Heating a house with oil, one year
items.scope: ≈2,000 L of heating oil (150 m², older Swiss house) × ≈3.2 kg per litre incl. fuel production.
items.summary: About 6 t a year: half a Swiss resident's whole footprint, just for heat.
tips: Replacing an oil boiler with a heat pump is usually the single largest cut a Swiss household can make (≈90%).

items.name: Heating a house with gas, one year
items.scope: ≈20,000 kWh of gas × ≈0.23 kg/kWh incl. upstream methane leaks.
items.summary: About a quarter less than oil, still a few tonnes.

items.name: Heating a house with a heat pump, one year
items.scope: ≈20,000 kWh of heat ÷ coefficient of performance ≈3.5 ≈ 5,700 kWh of electricity. Low end on Swiss production mix, central on Swiss consumption mix, high end on a coal-heavy grid.
items.summary: About a tenth of oil on Swiss power.

items.name: Cotton T-shirt
items.scope: Cotton growing, spinning, dyeing, sewing, transport, washing over its life.
items.summary: A few kg; textile mills run largely on coal in Asia.
tips: Wear it more often: doubling the wears halves the footprint per wear.

items.name: Pair of jeans
items.scope: Levi's 501 life-cycle study: cotton, fabric, manufacture, transport, and washing and drying over its life.
items.summary: About 33 kg, over a third of it from washing and drying.
tips: Wash jeans every ten wears, cold, and skip the dryer.

items.name: Running shoes
items.scope: Cradle-to-grave (MIT study of a typical synthetic running shoe); manufacturing energy is most of it.
items.summary: About 14 kg, two-thirds from the factory.

items.name: Paperback book
items.scope: Paper, printing, distribution; higher if unsold copies are pulped.
items.summary: About a kilo, roughly 20 hours of video streaming.

items.name: Plastic bottle (0.5 L PET)
items.scope: Plastic production and bottle forming; disposal adds a little (more if burned).
items.summary: About 80 g, compared with almost nothing for tap water.

items.name: Christmas tree (real)
items.scope: Growing, transport and disposal. Burned or chipped ≈3.5 kg; sent to landfill, where it rots to methane, ≈16 kg.
items.summary: A few kg if it is chipped or burned afterwards.

items.name: Christmas tree (artificial)
items.scope: Plastic and metal manufacture in Asia and shipping.
items.summary: Needs about 10 years of reuse to beat a real tree that is chipped afterwards.

items.name: 1 tonne of steel
items.scope: World average, cradle-to-gate (worldsteel). Low end: recycled scrap in an electric arc furnace on clean power; high end: coal blast furnace.
items.summary: About 1.9 t of CO₂ per tonne: steel weighs about its own weight in CO₂.

items.name: 1 tonne of cement
items.scope: Cradle-to-gate. About 60% comes from the chemistry itself (limestone releasing CO₂), not fuel, so clean energy alone cannot fix it.
items.summary: About 0.6 t per tonne. A cubic metre of concrete is roughly 0.25–0.35 t.

items.name: 1 tonne of primary aluminium
items.scope: Mine to ingot, global average (International Aluminium Institute). Hydro-powered smelters ≈4 t; coal-powered ≈20 t. Recycled aluminium needs about 5% of the energy.
items.summary: About 16 t of CO₂e per tonne: the most carbon-intensive common metal, and the case for recycling cans.

items.name: 1 tonne of plastic
items.scope: Cradle-to-gate for common polymers. Incineration at end of life adds up to about 2.7 t more.
items.summary: About 2.5 t per tonne, more if it is burned afterwards.

items.name: Coal power, worldwide
items.scope: Direct CO₂ from burning coal for electricity and heat (IEA).
items.summary: ≈10.5 Gt: about a fifth of all greenhouse gases, the largest single source on the planet.
items.context: Coal still makes about a third of the world's electricity, mostly in China and India. Every coal plant replaced by nuclear, wind or solar is the fastest-acting cut available.

items.name: A 1 GW coal plant for a year
items.scope: Generation × ≈950 g CO₂/kWh life cycle.
items.summary: ≈6 Mt a year: the domestic emissions of about 1.5 million Swiss residents, from one plant.

items.name: A 1 GW gas plant for a year
items.scope: Generation × ≈430–490 g CO₂e/kWh life cycle incl. upstream methane (UNECE).
items.summary: About half of coal, still about 3 Mt a year.

items.name: A 1 GW nuclear plant for a year
items.scope: Life cycle incl. mining, enrichment, construction and decommissioning (UNECE ≈5.1–6.4 g/kWh).
items.summary: ≈0.05 Mt a year: about 130 times less than the same coal plant, for more electricity.
items.context: Gösgen alone makes roughly 8 TWh a year, about 14% of Swiss electricity.

items.name: Road transport, worldwide
items.scope: Direct CO₂ from cars, trucks, buses and two-wheelers (IEA).
items.summary: ≈6 Gt: about three-quarters of transport emissions, and over 10% of the total.

items.name: Aviation, worldwide
items.scope: CO₂ from jet fuel ≈0.95 Gt (≈2.5% of energy CO₂). Including contrails and NOx, aviation's warming effect is roughly 2–3× its CO₂ (high end).
items.summary: ≈1 Gt of CO₂, and among the fastest-growing sources (international aviation +6% in 2024).
items.context: About 1% of people cause about half of aviation's emissions.

items.name: Shipping, worldwide
items.scope: International and domestic shipping, CO₂e (IMO 4th GHG study).
items.summary: ≈1 Gt, about 2–3% of the total, carrying around 80% of world trade by volume.

items.name: Steel industry, worldwide
items.scope: ≈1.9 Gt of steel × ≈1.9 t CO₂ per tonne (worldsteel), direct plus electricity.
items.summary: ≈3.6 Gt: about 7% of the total, more than all the world's aviation and shipping together.

items.name: Cement industry, worldwide
items.scope: Direct CO₂ from clinker chemistry and kiln fuel (IEA).
items.summary: ≈2.5 Gt: if cement were a country it would rank fourth, after China, the US and India.

items.name: Plastics, whole life cycle, worldwide
items.scope: Production, conversion and end of life (OECD Global Plastics Outlook, 2019 data); 90% from production.
items.summary: ≈1.8 Gt, about 3.4% of the total, and on course to double by 2060 without policy.

items.name: Fashion and textiles, worldwide
items.scope: Fibre to retail; estimates range from 1.2 Gt (Ellen MacArthur Foundation) to 2.1 Gt (McKinsey, ≈4%).
items.summary: Roughly 1–2 Gt, similar to aviation or shipping.

items.name: Livestock, worldwide
items.scope: Whole supply chains incl. feed, land-use change, methane from digestion and manure (FAO GLEAM, 2015 reference year).
items.summary: ≈6.2 Gt CO₂e: about 12% of human emissions, as much as all road transport.
items.context: Methane is short-lived but strong (≈80× CO₂ over 20 years), so cutting it slows warming quickly.

items.name: Cattle (beef and dairy), worldwide
items.scope: Cattle share (≈62%) of FAO livestock supply-chain emissions.
items.summary: ≈3.8 Gt: cattle alone emit more than the whole steel industry.

items.name: Rice paddies, worldwide
items.scope: Mostly methane from flooded fields; estimates vary with the inventory used.
items.summary: Around 1 Gt CO₂e, about 2% of the total, similar to all shipping.
tips: Alternate wetting and drying of paddies cuts methane by roughly a third to a half.

items.name: Methane from oil, gas and coal
items.scope: ≈120 Mt of methane from fossil-fuel operations (IEA Global Methane Tracker) × ≈30 (100-year GWP).
items.summary: ≈3.6 Gt CO₂e, much of it avoidable at low or negative cost because captured gas can be sold.
items.context: About 40% of these emissions could be avoided at no net cost, according to the IEA; satellites now detect large leaks directly.

items.name: Deforestation and land-use change
items.scope: Net CO₂ from land-use change (Global Carbon Budget bookkeeping method). Not in the sector pie, which excludes land use.
items.summary: ≈4 Gt: mostly tropical forest cleared for cattle, soy, palm oil and cocoa.

items.name: Air conditioning, worldwide
items.scope: CO₂ from electricity for space cooling (IEA); refrigerant leaks add more.
items.summary: ≈1 Gt and rising fast in hot, growing economies: more than all data centres five times over.

items.name: Militaries, worldwide (estimated)
items.scope: Estimated at about 5.5% of global emissions incl. supply chains (Scientists for Global Responsibility); military emissions are largely exempt from UN reporting, so the uncertainty is large.
items.summary: Possibly the size of a large industrial sector, and the least reported.

items.name: Average person, world
items.scope: Computed: 54.1 Gt (excl. land use) ÷ 8.2 billion people.
items.summary: About 6.6 t, but very unequal: the richest 10% cause about half of emissions.

items.name: Average Swiss resident
items.scope: Consumption-based footprint incl. imported goods (Federal Office for the Environment). Counting only emissions inside Switzerland gives about 4 t, among the lowest in Europe thanks to hydro and nuclear power.
items.summary: About 13 t once imports are counted: two-thirds of a Swiss footprint is emitted abroad.
items.context: Typical big items: heating (if fossil), flights, cars, meat and dairy, and imported goods.

items.name: Average US resident
items.scope: Computed: 6.02 Gt territorial ÷ ≈340 million people.
items.summary: About 18 t, nearly three times the world average.

items.name: Average Chinese resident
items.scope: Computed: ≈16 Gt territorial ÷ 1.41 billion. Includes making goods exported to other countries.
items.summary: About 11 t, above the EU average; part of it is manufacturing for export.

items.name: Average Indian resident
items.scope: Computed: 4.51 Gt ÷ ≈1.45 billion.
items.summary: About 3 t, under half the world average, but India had the largest absolute rise in 2024.

items.name: 1.5 °C-compatible lifestyle, 2030
items.scope: Per-person lifestyle footprint target for 2030 consistent with 1.5 °C (Hot or Cool Institute 1.5-Degree Lifestyles); falling to 0.7 t by 2050.
items.summary: About 2.5 t: one long-haul return flight nearly uses it up.
